name: Welding helmets, goggles and filter lenses
summary: Helmets, hand shields and goggles with dark filter lenses that block the UV, infrared and glare of welding and cutting; the shade must suit the job.
uses: Stick welding, OSHA minimum shade: 7 under 60 A, 8 at 60–160 A, 10 at 160–250 A, 11 above (OSHA 1910.133); ANSI/AWS suggest 10, 12, 14 for the top three bands (OSHA FS-3499)
Other minimums: MIG and flux-core 7 under 60 A, 10 above; TIG 8 up to 150 A, 10 above; plasma cutting 8–10. Start darker (OSHA 1910.133)
Gas welding 4–6, oxy-fuel cutting 3–5, torch brazing 3 (OSHA 1910.133): gas-welding goggles suit these, never arc welding (CCOHS welding PPE)
Sparks, spatter and slag on face and eyes; wear safety glasses or goggles underneath, above all for chipping slag (OSHA FS-3499; HSE welding)
Helpers and watchers need the same shade or a screen (CCOHS welding PPE; HSE welding): a few seconds of arc light can cause arc eye (CCOHS welding radiation)
Doesn't stop fumes: HSE asks for extraction, then a respirator where that can't control them (HSE welding); not electrical arc-flash gear unless arc-rated (OSHA 1910.269)
identify: Passive helmets have a fixed dark filter plate behind a clear outer cover lens, with a clear retainer lens inside to stop broken filter pieces reaching the eye (CCOHS welding PPE). Auto-darkening helmets have an LCD cartridge that rests at a light shade and darkens when its sensors see an arc. For example, the Lincoln Viking 3350 rests at shade 3.5, darkens to 5–13 in 1/25,000 s, has four sensors, a solar cell and one CR2450 lithium coin cell, and blocks UV and infrared whether light or dark (Lincoln Viking manual). Some have sealed batteries, others replaceable ones (EHS Today ADF). Gas-welding goggles have light shades for oxy-fuel work only (CCOHS welding PPE). Marks: the filter carries its shade number; US helmets should meet Z87.1 (EHS Today ADF), and in Canada CSA Z94.3 class 3 is helmets and class 4 hand shields (CCOHS welding PPE). Europe: fixed filters to EN 169 are marked on the edge, protection class first (uvex EN 166); auto-darkening filters to EN 379 show four optical classes such as 1/1/1/1, 1 best and 3 worst (Lincoln optical clarity). Not welding filters: sunglasses, smoked plastic and blue or tinted grinding glasses (CCOHS welding PPE; AWS shade chart).
test: Check the shell, filter and both clear cover lenses for cracks before each use; stop using a cracked auto-darkening filter, as its UV and infrared protection may be gone (Lincoln Viking manual). Never weld without the inside and outside clear lenses; replace them when spattered, pitted or hazy (Lincoln Viking manual; CCOHS welding PPE). Auto-darkening check: press TEST if fitted; then face a bright light and flick your fingers over the sensors: the lens should darken each time they are uncovered; a torch striker sparked in front also works (Lincoln Viking manual). If it won't darken, fit a fresh battery, clean the sensors, solar cell and cover lens, and check it isn't set to grind, which is for grinding only and never for welding (Lincoln Viking manual). The Viking is rated for −10 to 55 °C (Lincoln Viking manual), so test again in the cold. Fit: the helmet should sit close and stay down, and no arc light from behind should reach the filter (Lincoln Viking manual; CCOHS welding PPE). Keep glass filters from knocks and sudden temperature changes, which crack them (CCOHS welding PPE).

decay.note: Shells and fixed glass filters keep unless knocked or cracked. Auto-darkening filters with batteries you can't replace are expected to last 5–7 years; ones with a coin cell last longer with spares (EHS Today ADF). Spare cells and clear cover lenses run out.

improvise: There is no safe home-made arc filter. CCOHS says never use modified glasses, sunglasses, smoked plastic or other materials instead of proper welding lenses, and never use gas-welding goggles for arc welding (CCOHS welding PPE); its words 'other materials' take in smoked glass and exposed photo film too, though CCOHS does not name them. OSHA notes ordinary sunglasses aren't designed for welding protection (OSHA sunglasses letter); even for looking at the sun they pass hundreds to thousands of times too much light (AAS ISO 12312-2). What does work: a proper filter of the right shade from another helmet, fitted with a clear cover lens outside and a clear retainer inside (CCOHS welding PPE). OSHA says filter glasses under a helmet may let the helmet's shade be lowered, if the combined shade numbers equal the table value; if unsure, go darker (OSHA FS-3499). Without a filter, don't strike an arc or watch one. Protect bystanders with an opaque screen; HSE knows of no clear curtain that meets the screen standard (HSE welding).
